content: TEAD1, also known as Transcriptional Enhancer Factor TEF-1 or TEA domain family member 1, is a protein encoded by the TEAD1 gene in humans. It was the first identified member of the TEAD family of transcription factors. Structure All TEAD family members share a highly conserved DNA-binding domain called the TEA domain. This domain recognizes a consensus DNA sequence, 5’-CATTCCA/T-3’, referred to as the MCAT element. The three-dimensional structure of the TEA domain has been elucidated, revealing a conformation similar to that of the homeodomain, consisting of three alpha helices (H1, H2, and H3). The H3 helix is critical for DNA binding. Additionally, TEAD1 contains another conserved domain at its C-terminus, known as the YAP1-binding domain, which facilitates the binding of cofactors. TEAD proteins cannot independently induce gene expression and require association with cofactors to exert their function. Tissue Distribution TEAD1 is expressed in various tissues, including skeletal muscle, pancreas, placenta, lung, and heart. Orthologs TEAD proteins are conserved across many organisms, performing diverse functions under different names. For instance: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, TEC-1 regulates the transposable element TY1 and is involved in pseudohyphal growth under nutrient-poor conditions. In Aspergillus nidulans, the TEA domain protein ABAA regulates conidiophore differentiation. In Drosophila, the transcription factor Scalloped is essential for wing disc development, cell survival, and growth. In Xenopus, the TEAD1 ortholog regulates muscle differentiation. Function TEAD1 plays critical roles in: Heart development, including myocardium differentiation. Skeletal muscle development, such as the regulation of alpha-actin in skeletal muscles. Smooth muscle development, including the regulation of alpha-actin in smooth muscles. Regulation of myosin heavy chain genes and cardiac muscle genes like troponin T and I. Control of cell proliferation and apoptosis. Post-Transcriptional Modifications TEAD1 undergoes several post-translational modifications: Protein Kinase A (PKA) phosphorylates TEAD1 at serine 102, which is essential for the transcriptional activation of the α-MyHC gene. Protein Kinase C (PKC) phosphorylates TEAD1 on serine and threonine residues near the last alpha loop of the TEA domain, reducing its binding to the GTIIC enhancer. TEAD1 can be palmitoylated on a conserved cysteine at its C-terminus, a modification critical for proper protein folding and stability. Cofactors TEAD proteins require cofactors to activate the transcription of target genes. TEAD1 interacts with all members of the SRC family of steroid receptor coactivators. In HeLa cells, TEAD1 and SRC together induce gene expression. TEAD1 also interacts with PARP (Poly-ADP ribose polymerase) to regulate smooth muscle alpha-actin expression. PARP can ADP-ribosylate TEAD proteins, modifying chromatin to favor transcription through histone modifications. TEAD1 and SRF (Serum Response Factor) jointly regulate gene expression. TEAD proteins also physically interact with MEF2 (Myocyte Enhancer Factor 2), where MEF2 binding to DNA enhances TEAD1 recruitment to adjacent MCAT sequences, leading to repression of MLC2v and βMHC promoters. TEAD1 also interacts with the phosphoprotein MAX, forming a complex that regulates alpha-myosin heavy chain (α-MHC) gene expression. The Vestigial-like (VGLL) proteins interact with all TEADs, though their precise function remains poorly understood. TEAD/VGLL1 complexes promote anchorage-independent cell proliferation in prostate cancer cell lines, suggesting a role in cancer progression. VGLL2 interaction with TEAD1 activates muscle promoters during C2C12 differentiation and enhances MyoD-mediated myogenesis in 10T1/2 cells. The TEAD/VGLL4 complex acts as a default transcriptional repressor. TEAD proteins also interact with YAP (Yes-Associated Protein) and TAZ (a paralog of YAP), which are transcriptional coactivators. These interactions, demonstrated both in vitro and in vivo, enhance TEAD transcriptional activity. YAP/TAZ are effectors of the Hippo tumor suppressor pathway, which restricts organ growth by regulating cell proliferation and promoting apoptosis in mammals and Drosophila. Role in Cancer TEAD1 is dysregulated in several cancers. For example: In Kaposi sarcoma, TEAD1 levels are increased 300-fold. Elevated TEAD expression is observed in basal-like breast cancers, fallopian tube carcinoma, and germ cell tumors. Conversely, TEAD expression is decreased in other breast cancer subtypes, as well as in renal and bladder cancers. This dual role may be attributed to the differential regulation of target genes by TEAD transcription factors. Recent studies have shown that TEAD1 and YAP in ovarian cancer can induce cell stemness and chemoresistance. Genetic variants of TEAD proteins and YAP are enriched in certain cancers, further implicating their role in tumorigenesis.
